uncited: **Inputs:** Two registered volume datasets $X$ and $Y$ (intensity values), pre-defined 1D transfer functions $TF_X$ and $TF_Y$ (colors and opacities), and a target distribution definition.
**Outputs:** A fused multimodal transfer function defining a single color $c(x,y)$ and opacity $\alpha(x,y,g)$ for every voxel based on its intensity pair $(x,y)$ and fused gradient $g$.
**Intensity Bins:** The continuous intensity values of $X$ and $Y$ are discretized into bins $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ using a non-regular binning algorithm (see Binning).
The joint space is $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$.
**Information Maps:** Two 3D volumes per dataset, storing values $I_2(x;Y)$ and $I_3(x;Y)$ for each voxel, shifted so the minimum is 0.
**Joint Histogram:** A 3D histogram (or binned equivalent) counting occurrences of intensity pairs $(x,y)$ and potentially gradient values $g$.
**Visibility Distribution:** A probability distribution $p(b|v)$ or $p(b)$ over bins $\mathcal{B}$ for specific viewpoints or all viewpoints.
**Reference Selection:** Select the reference dataset (e.g., $X$) based on contrast.
Compute the mean local variance of intensities in a small window for each dataset (using segmented volumes for normalization if available).
*   The clustering merges bins of $X$ by minimizing the loss of mutual information with $Y$.
*   For each voxel with intensities $x$ (from $X$) and $y$ (from $Y$), compute the fused color $c(x,y)$.
*   **Target Distribution:** Define the target distribution $q(b)$ based on user preference.
*   *Occurrence:* $q(b) = \frac{occur(b)}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} occur(i)}$
*   *Gradient-weighted:* $q(b) = \frac{grad(b) occur(b)}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} (grad(i) occur(i))}$
*   *Importance-weighted:* $q(b) = \frac{\text{imp}(b) grad(b) occur(b)}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} (\text{imp}(i) grad(i) occur(i))}$
*   **Divergence Calculation:** Compute the divergence between visibility and target.
*   *Viewpoint Informational Divergence (VID):* $D_{KL}(p(B|v), q(B)) = \sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}} p(b|v) \log \frac{p(b|v)}{q(b)}$.
*   **Time Complexity:** The binning step is greedy hierarchical clustering.
The opacity optimization involves iterative ray casting for visibility estimation.
Performance depends heavily on the number of bins and viewpoints.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Requires storing joint histograms, information maps, and gradient volumes.
Binning reduces the joint histogram size significantly.
*   **Strengths:** Automates TF design; handles multimodal data effectively; preserves structures from both modalities; binning improves accuracy and reduces computational load.
*   **When to use:** When automatic fusion of two registered modalities is needed and manual TF design is too complex or time-consuming.
*   **When not to use:** When interpretability of specific colors is critical and cannot be mitigated by side-by-side visualization; when data is not registered.
It extends the work of Ruiz et al. [4] which handled single-modality opacity optimization, by defining an information channel between two input data sets.
The binning algorithm is based on the agglomerative information bottleneck method by Bardera et al. [33].
